title: Blocking acrylic crochet
subtitle: How steam blocking and wet blocking behave differently on synthetic yarn
excerpt: Acrylic does not wet-block like wool. The correct method is steam, but applied carefully. Use the wrong amount of heat and the yarn goes limp and loses all resilience.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book. Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins).

glossaryTerms.definition: The process of wetting or steaming a finished piece and shaping it to measurements while damp or under heat, so it dries or cools in the correct dimensions.
A blocking method that uses steam from an iron held above the fabric to relax the fibres without wetting them. Suitable for acrylic and heat-stable synthetics.

content.text: Acrylic yarn does not respond to water the way wool does. Wet
leaves an acrylic piece looking and feeling the same as before. The method that works on acrylic is

, which uses heat and moisture together to relax synthetic fibres into a new position. Applied correctly it opens up lace and evens out tension. Applied incorrectly it permanently kills the yarn's bounce.

items.name: Blocking mat
items.note: A foam interlocking mat or dedicated blocking board

items.name: Rust-proof pins
items.note: T-pins or blocking wires for lace

items.name: Steam iron or clothes steamer
items.note: Must produce a good volume of steam

items.name: Pressing cloth
items.note: A cotton cloth to protect the surface of delicate stitches

content.text: Lay the piece on the blocking mat. Pin it to the required measurements if shaping is needed.
Set the iron to the steam setting, no hotter than a low-medium heat. Too much heat kills acrylic permanently.
Hold the iron 5 to 10 cm above the surface. Do not press down onto the fabric. Move the iron steadily over the piece, letting the steam pass through.
Leave the piece pinned until it has cooled completely. The fibres set in the new position as they cool, not while they are hot.
Remove pins after the piece is cool and dry.
When acrylic does not need blocking

Amigurumi and tightly-worked toys do not benefit from blocking and should not be steamed. The dense fabric provides its own structure, and steam can distort stuffed pieces. Flat squares, shawls, and garment pieces are the main candidates.

items.symptom: The fabric feels limp and flat after blocking and does not spring back
items.cause: Too much heat was applied, or the iron touched the surface. Acrylic softens permanently above a certain temperature.
items.fix: The damage cannot be reversed. On future pieces, hold the iron higher and use a lower heat setting. Test on a small swatch first.

items.symptom: The piece looks the same after steam blocking
items.cause: The iron produced very little steam, or was moved too quickly to let the steam penetrate the fabric.
items.fix: Fill the iron fully with water and wait until it is producing a good volume of steam before starting. Move it more slowly over each section.

items.symptom: The shape pulled back after removing the pins
items.cause: The piece was unpinned before it had fully cooled. Acrylic sets on cooling, not on contact with steam.
items.fix: Leave pins in place until the piece is completely cool to the touch, which takes at least 30 minutes.

content.text: Test steam blocking on a swatch before applying it to a finished garment. Work a 15 cm square, steam half of it, and leave the other half unblocked. Compare the two sides after cooling to see the difference in stitch definition before committing to the full piece.
